The road out of Bakersfield runs flat and mean for ninety-one miles before it gives you anything to look at, and by the time I hit the county line at 4:15 in the afternoon the thermometer bolted to the dash of the rented Buick read 108 degrees and climbing. The air conditioner had quit outside Delano. I had four gallons of water, a carton of Luckys, $63 in cash, and a press credential that expired in November.

Nobody had told me about the smell.

It arrives about six miles before the feedlot does — a thick, sweet, ammoniac wall that gets into the upholstery and stays there. The county has been fighting about it since 1997. There are four separate lawsuits, three of which have been dismissed, and a zoning variance signed on a Thursday afternoon in March by a man who sold his interest in the parcel eleven weeks later for $2.1 million.

That is the whole story, if you want it in one sentence. Everything else is weather.

I sat in the lot behind the Chevron and watched the trucks come through, forty-two of them between five and seven, each one hauling nine hundred head of something that had been alive that morning. The men who drove them were courteous and tired. One of them, a heavyset kid from Tulare with a burn scar running the length of his left forearm, told me he'd been on the route four years and no longer noticed the smell at all. He said it like a man confessing to something.

There was a time when this valley grew stone fruit and the towns along 99 had names people said with some affection. My father drove this road in a green Ford in 1961 and stopped at a stand outside McFarland for peaches that cost him a dollar. He told me about it more than once. He is dead now and the stand is a Dollar General with a sun-bleached banner in the window, and the peaches come from Chile.

The variance was public record the entire time. Anyone could have read it. Almost nobody did, and the ones who did were paid not to mind, and the kid from Tulare will be driving that route until his lungs give out or the market moves, whichever comes first — and the man who signed the paper has a house in Montecito with a view of the water and an opinion about the importance of local agriculture that he shares, at length, on request.
